2.43 Storage of water in Amistad Reservoir began on May 31, 1968 and the reservoir first reached conservation pool elevation of 1117.0 feet on August 16, 1972. During the initial filling period, releases were made continuously to satisfy downstream users at rates varying from 100 to 11,000 cfs. No flood releases were made during this period. During the period between August 16, 1972 and June 30, 1974, releases from Amistad Reservoir ranged from a minimum of 20 cfs to a maximum of 9,000 cfs with several periods during which no releases were made. Most of the releases during this period were made to furnish water to downstream users.
2.44 A characteristic of historic operations (and an expected characteristic of future operations without the proposed action) is the relatively gradual variation in conservation water releases from Amistad Reservoir. Such releases have often been continuous for several weeks to several months at a time and do not normally undergo rapid variation or fluctuation. In general, conservation water release rates are not changed more than once per week under present operating criteria.
Eagle Pass Project
2.45 The Maverick County Water Control and Improvement District No. 1 project is located downstream from Amistad Dam near Eagle Pass, Texas. This project diverts water from the Rio Grande by a diversion dam into a 31.5 mile gravity canal system for irrigation and hydroelectric generation at the Central Power and Light's Eagle Pass plant. The capacity of the canal is 1,500 second-feet, of which 600 second-feet is used for irrigation and 900 second-feet for power generation. Three 3,200 kW generating units provide a total capacity of 9,600 kW. The power is delivered through necessary switches and transformers to the high voltage transmission system supplying the local area, interconnected plants, and service areas of the Central Power and Light Company (TWDB, 1968).
Archeological Characteristics
2.46 There are over 350 known archeological sites and many historic sites, mostly railroad camps of the mid 1800's, on the US side of the reservoir basin in Val Verde County. There are also a number of sites on the Mexican side as well as on both sides below the damsite. The largest and most spectacular of the prehistoric sites are the rockshelters which are confined mainly to the lower Pecos River, Mile Canyon, and adjacent stretches of the Rio Grande. Panels of unique and excellent pictographs, many in a good state of preservation, are found throughout the Amistad area in these large shelters and beneath overhangs where they have been protected from climatic elements. Also there are numerous open surface sites and some terrace sites which are buried in alluvium and have well preserved stratigraphy. These archeological resources are significant in that they offer a record of prehistoric cultural development in Southwest Texas and the northern Coahuila area (Mexico). To quote Graham and Davis (1958): "In several respects the Diablo (Amistad) Reservoir is one of the unique archeological regions of North America. Probably no area of comparable size can boast of so rich a series of archeological and pictographic sites." The Amistad pictographs are archeologically unique in that they are very abundant in a relatively small geographic area. Paintings, petrogylyphs, and painted pebbles have been recovered from some sites. The pictographs depict anthropomorphic figures, naturalistic representations, and a variety of geometric forms.
